claim: Vascular dysfunctions are a common feature of multiple age-related diseases.
source: Vascular dysfunctions are a common feature of multiple age-related diseases.
evidence: This is a general statement about vascular dysfunction and aging that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: iVECs induced from old donors revealed upregulation of GSTM1 and PALD1, genes linked to oxidative stress, inflammation and endothelial junction stability, as vascular aging markers.
source: iVECs induced from old donors revealed upregulation of GSTM1 and PALD1, genes linked to oxidative stress, inflammation and endothelial junction stability, as vascular aging markers.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data presented in the manuscript comparing iVECs from young vs. old donors, as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A functional assay performed on PALD1 KD VECs demonstrated a recovery in vascular permeability.
source: A functional assay performed on PALD1 KD VECs demonstrated a recovery in vascular permeability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from knockdown experiments shown in Figure 2K.

claim: iSMCs from HGPS donors overexpressed bone morphogenetic protein (BMP)−4, which plays a key role in both vascular calcification and endothelial barrier damage observed in HGPS.
source: We found that iSMCs from HGPS donors overexpressed bone morphogenetic protein (BMP)−4, which plays a key role in both vascular calcification and endothelial barrier damage observed in HGPS.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data comparing HGPS vs. healthy iSMCs (Figure 3A) and by established knowledge about BMP4's role in vascular pathology.

claim: BMP4 concentrations are higher in serum from HGPS vs. age-matched mice.
source: Strikingly, BMP4 concentrations are higher in serum from HGPS vs. age-matched mice.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Targeting BMP4 with blocking antibody recovered the functionality of the vascular barrier in vitro.
source: Furthermore, targeting BMP4 with blocking antibody recovered the functionality of the vascular barrier in vitro, hence representing a potential future therapeutic strategy to limit cardiovascular dysfunction in HGPS.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from antibody blocking experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: iVECs and iSMCs retain disease-related signatures, allowing modeling of vascular aging and HGPS in vitro.
source: These results show that iVECs and iSMCs retain disease-related signatures, allowing modeling of vascular aging and HGPS in vitro.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined RNAseq and functional data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Physiological and pathological aging represent a major risk factor for the onset of cardiovascular diseases, the leading cause of death worldwide.
source: Physiological and pathological aging represent a major risk factor for the onset of cardiovascular diseases, the leading cause of death worldwide (Benjamin et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Benjamin et al., 2019.

claim: Direct reprogramming of skin fibroblasts into functional cells was previously reported for blood progenitor cells, SMCs and VECs.
source: Among the available strategies, direct reprogramming of skin fibroblasts into functional cells was previously reported for blood progenitor cells (Szabo et al., 2010), SMCs (van Tuyn et al., 2005) and VECs (Han et al., 2014; Morita et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The differentiation process of iPS cells requires a mandatory transit through an embryonic-like state which was reported to reset the aging profile of the cells of origin.
source: Indeed, although iPS cells have significantly contributed to the discovery of novel disease mechanisms (Park et al., 2019) as well as to the pre-clinical screening of promising drug candidates (Zhang et al., 2019), the differentiation process of iPS cells requires a mandatory transit through an embryonic-like state which was reported to reset the aging profile of the cells of origin (Mertens et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mertens et al., 2015.

claim: Direct reprogramming from skin fibroblasts was shown to maintain the cellular signature of aging and to highlight critical factors of human aging in neurons.
source: Conversely, direct reprogramming from skin fibroblasts was shown to maintain the cellular signature of aging and to highlight critical factors of human aging in neurons (Mertens et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mertens et al., 2015.

claim: ETV2 alone was sufficient to in vitro reprogram human skin fibroblasts into functional VECs.
source: Strikingly, it was demonstrated that ETV2 alone, which is a master regulator of VEC development and early vasculogenesis (Qiu and Hirschi, 2019), was sufficient to in vitro reprogram human skin fibroblasts into functional VECs (Morita et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Morita et al., 2015.

claim: The induced expression of myocardin (MYOCD) was able to strongly induce both smooth and cardiac muscle genes in human foreskin fibroblasts and mesenchymal stem cells.
source: Similarly, the induced expression of myocardin (MYOCD) was able to strongly induce both smooth and cardiac muscle genes in human foreskin fibroblasts and mesenchymal stem cells (van Tuyn et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to van Tuyn et al., 2005.

claim: Directly reprogrammed cells, but not iPS cells, preserve the aging signature of the donor.
source: Since directly reprogrammed cells, but not iPS cells, preserve the aging signature of the donor (Mertens et al., 2015) and can be largely expanded from an easily obtained skin biopsy compared to other rare cell sources (e.g. blood-derived endothelial progenitor cells) (Mathur et al., 2019), we hypothesized that these cells could represent an effective tool to study cardiovascular aging and disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mertens et al., 2015 and Mathur et al., 2019.

claim: Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Syndrome (HGPS) is a rare age-related disease induced by mutation in the Lamin A/C gene.
source: In particular, Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Syndrome (HGPS) is a rare age-related disease induced by mutation in the Lamin A/C gene (Prokocimer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Prokocimer et al., 2013.

claim: The Lamin A/C mutation in HGPS not only alters the architecture of the nuclear envelope but also impacts the genome organization and gene expression leading to severe cardiovascular damage.
source: This mutation not only alters the architecture of the nuclear envelope but also impacts the genome organization and gene expression leading to severe cardiovascular damage (e.g. atherosclerosis, vascular calcification), which is responsible for the premature death of patients at an average age of 14 years.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about HGPS pathology.

claim: HGPS patients die prematurely at an average age of 14 years.
source: This mutation not only alters the architecture of the nuclear envelope but also impacts the genome organization and gene expression leading to severe cardiovascular damage (e.g. atherosclerosis, vascular calcification), which is responsible for the premature death of patients at an average age of 14 years.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about HGPS.

claim: iSMCs expressed cell-identity markers including alpha smooth muscle actin (αSMA) (expressed by about 70% cells) and calponin (expressed by about 80% cells).
source: iSMCs expressed cell-identity markers including alpha smooth muscle actin (αSMA) (Figure 1A, expressed by about 70% cells) and calponin (Figure 1B, expressed by about 80% cells), both in monoculture and when co-cultured with VECs (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: αSMA-expressing iSMCs contributed to the formation of microvascular networks in 3D fibrin matrices.
source: Importantly, αSMA-expressing iSMCs contributed to the formation of microvascular networks in 3D fibrin matrices (Figure 1D), thus mimicking the behavior of fibroblasts and differentiated mesenchymal stem cells observed in previous vascular models developed by our (Bersini et al., 2016; Jeon et al., 2014) and other groups (Zheng et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 1D and citations to previous studies.

claim: No differences were found in terms of vascular area fraction when VECs were co-cultured with fibroblasts or iSMCs.
source: In particular, no differences were found in terms of vascular area fraction when VECs were co-cultured with fibroblasts or iSMCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: CD31+ iVECs were able to self-assemble into vessel-like structures when co-cultured with skin fibroblasts or iSMCs in 3D fibrin matrices.
source: In parallel, we found that CD31+ iVECs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) were able to self-assemble into vessel-like structures when co-cultured with skin fibroblasts (Figure 1E) or iSMCs (Video 1) in 3D fibrin matrices.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 1E and Video 1.

claim: The vessel-like structures formed by iVECs were patent, as demonstrated by cross-sectional views of the lumens.
source: These vessel-like structures were patent, as demonstrated by cross-sectional views of the lumens (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 1F.

claim: The SMC identity gene ACTA2 was enriched in both reprogrammed cells and primary vascular cells when compared to the original skin fibroblasts.
source: Strikingly, we found that the SMC identity gene ACTA2 (Figure 1G, cluster 2) and multiple endothelial-specific genes (e.g. FLT1, KDR, CDH5, TIE2, ROBO4, NECTIN2) (Figure 1I, cluster 2) were enriched in both reprogrammed cells and primary vascular cells when compared to the original skin fibroblasts.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Multiple endothelial-specific genes (e.g. FLT1, KDR, CDH5, TIE2, ROBO4, NECTIN2) were enriched in both reprogrammed cells and primary vascular cells when compared to the original skin fibroblasts.
source: Strikingly, we found that the SMC identity gene ACTA2 (Figure 1G, cluster 2) and multiple endothelial-specific genes (e.g. FLT1, KDR, CDH5, TIE2, ROBO4, NECTIN2) (Figure 1I, cluster 2) were enriched in both reprogrammed cells and primary vascular cells when compared to the original skin fibroblasts.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: iVECs expressed less CD31 and TJP1 compared to primary endothelial cells.
source: For example, iVECs expressed less CD31 and TJP1 compared to primary endothelial cells (Figure 1I, cluster 3).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The expression level of KDR was 6.62 log2FoldChange higher in primary VECs vs. fibroblasts and 6.38 log2FC higher in iVECs vs. fibroblasts.
source: However, the expression level of KDR (an important gene defining endothelial cell identity) was 6.62 log2FoldChange (FC) higher in primary VECs vs. fibroblasts and 6.38 log2FC higher in iVECs vs. fibroblasts.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data analysis.

claim: CDH5 was upregulated in both primary cells (log2FC = 6.7) and iVECs (log2FC = 4) compared to fibroblasts, although at different levels.
source: At the same time, another endothelial-specific gene (i.e. CDH5) was upregulated in both primary cells (log2FC = 6.7) and iVECs (log2FC = 4) compared to fibroblasts, although at different levels (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data in Supplementary file 5.

claim: Both primary and reprogrammed SMCs upregulated key identity genes including ACTA2 and MYH10 compared to fibroblasts.
source: Similarly, both primary and reprogrammed SMCs upregulated key identity genes including ACTA2 and MYH10 compared to fibroblasts (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data in Supplementary file 5.

claim: The expression of MYH10 was lower in reprogrammed vs. primary SMCs.
source: Notably, the expression of MYH10 was lower in reprogrammed vs. primary SMCs.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data analysis.

claim: Key skin fibroblast cell identity genes (e.g. FSP1, SLUG, TWIST1, TWIST2) were downregulated in both reprogrammed and primary vascular cells.
source: Furthermore, key skin fibroblast cell identity genes (e.g. FSP1, SLUG, TWIST1, TWIST2) (Figure 1G, cluster 4; Figure 1I, cluster 1) were downregulated in both reprogrammed and primary vascular cells (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1G, 1I and Supplementary file 5.

claim: iVECs upregulated genes linked to blood vessel morphogenesis and VE-cadherin-VEGF receptor complex when compared to fibroblasts.
source: Finally, gene ontology analysis revealed that iVECs upregulated genes linked to blood vessel morphogenesis and VE-cadherin-VEGF receptor complex when compared to fibroblasts (Figure 1J), while iSMCs upregulated genes associated with muscle contraction and muscle development (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 1J.

claim: iSMCs upregulated genes associated with muscle contraction and muscle development when compared to fibroblasts.
source: Finally, gene ontology analysis revealed that iVECs upregulated genes linked to blood vessel morphogenesis and VE-cadherin-VEGF receptor complex when compared to fibroblasts (Figure 1J), while iSMCs upregulated genes associated with muscle contraction and muscle development (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The majority of the markers expressed by reprogrammed cells remained fibroblast-like.
source: Taken together, the majority of the markers expressed by reprogrammed cells remained fibroblast-like.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNAseq data analysis presented.

claim: Reprogrammed SMCs and VECs expressed typical cell identity genes, self-organized into 3D vascular structures mimicking simple vascular networks and showed a global gene expression signature representing a gradual transition towards fully mature cells.
source: After carefully considering this critical point, we would like to highlight that reprogrammed SMCs and VECs expressed typical cell identity genes, self-organized into 3D vascular structures mimicking simple vascular networks and showed a global gene expression signature representing a gradual transition towards fully mature cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined RNAseq and imaging data presented.

claim: Directly reprogrammed, but not iPS cell-derived neurons, were able to retain the transcriptional aging signature of the donor.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that directly reprogrammed, but not iPS cell-derived neurons, were able to retain the transcriptional aging signature of the donor (Mertens et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mertens et al., 2015.

claim: Aging is characterized by a progressive decrease in the functionality of the endothelial barrier.
source: Aging is characterized by a progressive decrease in the functionality of the endothelial barrier (Palmer and Ousman, 2018), formation of atherosclerotic lesions, reduced contractility and calcifications of SMCs (Yao et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Palmer and Ousman, 2018.

claim: Aging is characterized by formation of atherosclerotic lesions, reduced contractility and calcifications of SMCs.
source: Aging is characterized by a progressive decrease in the functionality of the endothelial barrier (Palmer and Ousman, 2018), formation of atherosclerotic lesions, reduced contractility and calcifications of SMCs (Yao et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yao et al., 2013.

claim: The expression of MYOCD and ETV2 was comparable in reprogrammed cells derived from young and old donors.
source: It is important to highlight that the expression of MYOCD and ETV2 was comparable in reprogrammed cells derived from young and old donors (log2FC = 0.03 for MYOCD and log2FC = 0.19 for ETV2 comparing young and old cells; no statistical difference comparing young and old cells).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data analysis.

claim: DE analysis highlighted a set of genes (21 DE genes for iSMCs; 9 DE genes for iVECs) that changed according to the age of the donor.
source: DE analysis highlighted a set of genes (21 DE genes for iSMCs; 9 DE genes for iVECs) that changed according to the age of the donor for either iSMCs (Figure 2A) or iVECs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: The expression of a few cell identity genes in iSMCs or iVECs derived from young and old donors did not show obvious age-related differences.
source: We then analyzed the expression of a few cell identity genes in iSMCs or iVECs derived from young and old donors without finding obvious age-related differences (Supplementary file 6 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 6 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The reprogramming efficiency should not be affected by the age of the donor.
source: Together with the similar expression of MYOCD and ETV2 in cells derived from young and old donors, these data suggest that the reprogramming efficiency should not be affected by the age of the donor and that potential differences between young and old cells do not seem to be due to different levels of reprogramming.
evidence: This is an inference based on the gene expression data.

claim: iSMCs from older donors showed upregulation of bone morphogenetic protein 2 (BMP2), which is involved in the vascular calcification of blood vessels during aging and disease.
source: Intriguingly, among the 21 DE genes, iSMCs from older donors showed upregulation of bone morphogenetic protein 2 (BMP2), which is involved in the vascular calcification of blood vessels during aging and disease (Petsophonsakul et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data and a citation to Petsophonsakul et al., 2019.

claim: αSMA+ cells in human skin biopsies from old vs. young donors expressed higher levels of BMP2 (217.4 ± 10.9% vs. 100.0±10.4% after normalization).
source: Significantly, we found that αSMA+ cells in human skin biopsies from old (N = 2) vs. young (N = 2) donors expressed higher levels of BMP2 (217.4 ± 10.9% vs. 100.0±10.4% after normalization, Figure 2C and E; Videos 2 and 3), in agreement with the RNAseq findings.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C and 2E.

claim: The pattern of αSMA+ cells suggests that these cells are actually surrounding blood vessels rather than being isolated in the skin extracellular matrix.
source: Noteworthy, the pattern of αSMA+ cells suggests that these cells are actually surrounding blood vessels rather than being isolated in the skin extracellular matrix (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an inference based on imaging data in Figure 2E.

claim: iSMCs derived from an old donor (67 y.o.) showed higher expression of BMP2 compared to iSMCs from a young donor (19 y.o.) when co-cultured.
source: Finally, we co-cultured iSMCs generated from a young (19 y.o.) and an old (67 y.o.) donor finding higher expression of BMP2 in the iSMCs derived from the old donor (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), confirming observations seen with RNAseq and immunofluorescence of skin biopsies.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: GSTM1 is generally activated in presence of oxidative stress and inflammatory conditions.
source: GSTM1 is generally activated in presence of oxidative stress and inflammatory conditions (Lopes-Aguiar et al., 2017), while PALD1 is an endothelial-specific gene inhibiting endothelial junction stability (Nitzsche, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lopes-Aguiar et al., 2017.

claim: PALD1 is an endothelial-specific gene inhibiting endothelial junction stability.
source: GSTM1 is generally activated in presence of oxidative stress and inflammatory conditions (Lopes-Aguiar et al., 2017), while PALD1 is an endothelial-specific gene inhibiting endothelial junction stability (Nitzsche, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nitzsche, 2016.

claim: CD31+ VECs from old vs. young healthy donors expressed higher levels of PALD1 (194.9 ± 30.0% vs. 100.0±24.3% after normalization).
source: To test if these genes were actually dysregulated in human donors, we analyzed human skin biopsies and found that CD31+ VECs from old vs. young healthy donors indeed expressed higher levels of PALD1 (194.9 ± 30.0% vs. 100.0±24.3% after normalization, Figure 2D and F; Videos 4 and 5) and GSTM1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2D and 2F.

claim: CD31+ VECs from old vs. young healthy donors expressed higher levels of GSTM1.
source: To test if these genes were actually dysregulated in human donors, we analyzed human skin biopsies and found that CD31+ VECs from old vs. young healthy donors indeed expressed higher levels of PALD1 (194.9 ± 30.0% vs. 100.0±24.3% after normalization, Figure 2D and F; Videos 4 and 5) and GSTM1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The gene expression differences observed in directly reprogrammed cells partially recapitulate signatures of aging in humans.
source: This result shows that the gene expression differences observed in directly reprogrammed cells partially recapitulate signatures of aging in humans.
evidence: This is an inference based on the validation of RNAseq findings in human skin biopsies.

claim: DE analysis on primary VECs from mouse skin, brain and bone marrow highlighted a clear upregulation of GSTM1 and PALD1 in cells obtained from old (18 months) vs. young (3 months) animals.
source: Strikingly, DE analysis on primary VECs from mouse skin, brain and bone marrow also highlighted a clear upregulation of GSTM1 and PALD1 in cells obtained from old (18 months) vs. young (3 months) animals (N = 3 animals per condition, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Both PALD1 and GSTM1 might represent evolutionary conserved vascular aging markers.
source: Together, these data suggest that both PALD1 and GSTM1 might represent evolutionary conserved vascular aging markers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of similar upregulation in both human and mouse VECs.

claim: Abnormal expression of BMPs has been linked to vascular dysfunction.
source: Since abnormal expression of BMPs has been linked to vascular dysfunction (Cai et al., 2012; Csiszar et al., 2009) and upregulation of PALD1 to compromised VEC junctions (Nitzsche, 2016), we hypothesized that the identified DE genes might reflect a functional change in vascular permeability.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cai et al., 2012 and Csiszar et al., 2009.

claim: Upregulation of PALD1 has been linked to compromised VEC junctions.
source: Since abnormal expression of BMPs has been linked to vascular dysfunction (Cai et al., 2012; Csiszar et al., 2009) and upregulation of PALD1 to compromised VEC junctions (Nitzsche, 2016), we hypothesized that the identified DE genes might reflect a functional change in vascular permeability.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nitzsche, 2016.

claim: The presence of old vs. young iVECs lining the interface with the matrix channel increased the vascular permeability (146.1 ± 5.4% vs. 100.0±4.6% after normalization for old vs. young iVECs).
source: The presence of old vs. young iVECs (N = 3 donors per condition) lining the interface with the matrix channel increased the vascular permeability (146.1 ± 5.4% vs. 100.0±4.6% after normalization for old vs. young iVECs).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the microfluidic permeability assay.

claim: The difference in permeability can be explained by partial damage to cell-cell junctions, as indicated by the different pattern of Y658 VE-Cadherin in old vs. young iVECs.
source: The difference in permeability can be explained by partial damage to cell-cell junctions, as indicated by the different pattern of Y658 VE-Cadherin in old vs. young iVECs (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is an inference based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Permeability of young (131.9 ± 6.1%) and old (192.7 ± 7.1%) iVECs was significantly lower compared to fibroblasts (250.0 ± 12.1%), reaching values close to primary VECs (100.0 ± 4.7%).
source: Comparison with positive control (primary VECs lining the channel) and negative control (fibroblasts lining the channel) revealed that permeability of young (131.9 ± 6.1%) and old (192.7 ± 7.1%) iVECs was significantly lower compared to fibroblasts (250.0 ± 12.1%), reaching values close to primary VECs (100.0 ± 4.7%) (Figure 2I, data normalized to the permeability of primary VECs).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The presence of old vs. young iSMCs in the fibrin matrix channel induced a significant increase in the leakiness of the endothelial barrier (149.8 ± 11.3% vs. 100.0±4.7%, data normalized to young iSMCs).
source: Similarly, the presence of old vs. young iSMCs (N = 3 donors per condition) in the fibrin matrix channel induced a significant increase in the leakiness of the endothelial barrier (149.8 ± 11.3% vs. 100.0±4.7%, data normalized to young iSMCs).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the microfluidic permeability assay.

claim: iSMCs from young donors induced even lower levels of vascular permeability compared to primary SMCs (78.2 ± 3.7% vs. 100.0 ± 4.3%).
source: iSMCs from young donors induced even lower levels of vascular permeability compared to primary SMCs (78.2 ± 3.7% vs. 100.0 ± 4.3%) (Figure 2J, data normalized to primary SMCs), demonstrating that direct reprogramming generates functional cells which contribute to the maintenance of the vascular barrier.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Direct reprogramming generates functional cells which contribute to the maintenance of the vascular barrier.
source: iSMCs from young donors induced even lower levels of vascular permeability compared to primary SMCs (78.2 ± 3.7% vs. 100.0 ± 4.3%) (Figure 2J, data normalized to primary SMCs), demonstrating that direct reprogramming generates functional cells which contribute to the maintenance of the vascular barrier.
evidence: This is an inference based on the permeability data.

claim: iSMCs from young vs. old donors were more migratory, being able to reach the endothelial barrier at the interface with the 3D matrix.
source: Surprisingly, we also found that iSMCs from young vs. old donors were more migratory, being able to reach the endothelial barrier at the interface with the 3D matrix (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: PALD1 KD in VECs decreased vascular permeability compared to luciferase control (51.5 ± 3.4% vs. 100.0 ± 4.3%).
source: Collected data showed that PALD1 KD in VECs decreased vascular permeability compared to luciferase control (51.5 ± 3.4% vs. 100.0 ± 4.3%) (Figure 2K, data normalized to the permeability with luciferase control).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: KD of BMP2 in SMCs induced a weak, but reproducible, decrease in permeability compared to luciferase control (86.3 ± 3.8% vs. 100.0 ± 4.3%).
source: On the other side, KD of BMP2 in SMCs induced a weak, but reproducible, decrease in permeability compared to luciferase control (86.3 ± 3.8% vs. 100.0 ± 4.3%) (Figure 2L, data normalized to luciferase control).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Reprogramming induces a minimum set of transcriptional and functional features which allow to capture a fraction of the vascular changes occurring during aging and disease.
source: Overall, while we do not claim that reprogrammed cells are transcriptionally and functionally identical to primary cells, these data clearly demonstrate that reprogramming induces a minimum set of transcriptional and functional features which allow to capture a fraction of the vascular changes occurring during aging and disease.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined transcriptional and functional data.

claim: One of the main cardiovascular complications observed in HGPS is the loss of SMC coverage of blood vessels.
source: One of the main cardiovascular complications observed in HGPS is the loss of SMC coverage of blood vessels (Stehbens et al., 2001; Varga et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stehbens et al., 2001 and Varga et al., 2006.

claim: iPS cell-derived SMCs from a HGPS donor showed increased calcification and apoptosis when compared to cells obtained from a healthy donor.
source: In a recent tissue engineered blood vessel model, iPS cell-derived SMCs from a HGPS donor showed increased calcification and apoptosis when compared to cells obtained from a healthy donor (Atchison et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Atchison et al., 2017.

claim: RNAseq on iSMCs derived from healthy vs. HGPS donors revealed 93 DE genes.
source: Following the same strategy used to identify signatures of vascular aging, we performed RNAseq on iSMCs derived from N = 3 healthy donors vs. N = 8 HGPS donors (Supplementary file 1) revealing 93 DE genes (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: BMP4 is generally overexpressed during the early onset of vascular calcification.
source: Among the identified DE genes, we found upregulation of BMP4, which is generally overexpressed during the early onset of vascular calcification (Wei et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wei et al., 2018.

claim: Secreted BMP4 enhances the activation of the endothelium and induces production of reactive oxygen species by VECs, compromising the vascular barrier.
source: Moreover, secreted BMP4 enhances the activation of the endothelium and induces production of reactive oxygen species by VECs (Lowery and de Caestecker, 2010), compromising the vascular barrier.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lowery and de Caestecker, 2010.

claim: BMP4 was higher in healthy vs. HGPS donors below 11 years old, while a reverse trend was observed for children above 12 years old.
source: Interestingly, we found that BMP4 was higher in healthy vs. HGPS donors below 11 years old, while a reverse trend was observed for children above 12 years old (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was a significant decrease in the level of BMP4 in older vs. younger healthy individuals (p=0.04) which was lost in the HGPS samples.
source: Analyzing these data from an aging perspective, we found a significant decrease in the level of BMP4 in older vs. younger healthy individuals (p=0.04) which was lost in the HGPS samples.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of ELISA data.

claim: The level of BMP4 is high during early development, being a key regulator of musculo-skeletal system formation and vascularization.
source: Indeed, it is reported that the level of BMP4 is high during early development, being a key regulator of musculo-skeletal system formation and vascularization.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about BMP4 function.

claim: BMP4 decreases during late childhood/young adulthood and then increases again during physiological aging, as well as in pathological conditions including metabolic syndrome, leukemia or bone fractures.
source: BMP4 decreases during late childhood/young adulthood and then increases again during physiological aging (Meyers et al., 2016), as well as in pathological conditions including metabolic syndrome (Son et al., 2011), leukemia (Voeltzel et al., 2018) or bone fractures (van Baardewijk et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Meyers et al., 2016, Son et al., 2011, Voeltzel et al., 2018, and van Baardewijk et al., 2013.

claim: Blood from HGPS mouse models carrying the progerin mutation G609G revealed a higher level of BMP4 compared to age-matched healthy mice and extremely old mice.
source: Given the extremely limited number of available samples from HGPS patients, we then collected blood from HGPS mouse models carrying the progerin mutation G609G (N = 3, 13–14 weeks old) and we compared the level of circulating BMP4 with age-matched healthy mice (N = 3, 15 weeks old) as well as with extremely old mice (N = 5, about 2 years old). Collected data revealed a higher level of BMP4 in the blood of HGPS mice (Figure 3C), hence further corroborating the analyses performed on human samples.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Jagged 1-mediated Notch activation induces hyper-permeability of blood vessels in a model of diabetic retinopathy.
source: Indeed, recent studies demonstrated that Jagged 1-mediated Notch activation induces hyper-permeability of blood vessels in a model of diabetic retinopathy and that blocking Jagged 1 can prevent retinal edema (Miloudi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Miloudi et al., 2019.

claim: Blocking Jagged 1 can prevent retinal edema.
source: Indeed, recent studies demonstrated that Jagged 1-mediated Notch activation induces hyper-permeability of blood vessels in a model of diabetic retinopathy and that blocking Jagged 1 can prevent retinal edema (Miloudi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Miloudi et al., 2019.

claim: iSMCs from HGPS vs. healthy donors upregulated JAG1.
source: Intriguingly, we found that iSMCs from HGPS vs. healthy donors upregulated JAG1, suggesting its potential contribution in driving the pathological remodeling of blood vessels in HGPS patients.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The presence of HGPS iSMCs determined a significant increase in the vascular leakiness compared to young donors (197.4 ± 7.5% vs. 100.0±4.6% after normalization).
source: Strikingly, we found that the presence of HGPS iSMCs determined a significant increase in the vascular leakiness compared to young donors (197.4 ± 7.5% vs. 100.0±4.6% after normalization, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Treatment with antibodies blocking secreted BMP4 resulted in a significant decrease in the vascular leakiness (27.8 ± 1.6% vs. 100.0 ± 4.4% for BMP4 antibody after normalization).
source: Strikingly, we found a significant decrease in the vascular leakiness upon antibody treatment in both conditions compared to control (27.8 ± 1.6% vs. 100.0 ± 4.4% for BMP4 antibody after normalization and 61.5 ± 3.8% vs. 100.0 ± 4.4% for Jagged 1 antibody after normalization; Figure 3F and Videos 6, 7 and 8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Treatment with antibodies blocking Jagged 1 resulted in a significant decrease in the vascular leakiness (61.5 ± 3.8% vs. 100.0 ± 4.4% for Jagged 1 antibody after normalization).
source: Strikingly, we found a significant decrease in the vascular leakiness upon antibody treatment in both conditions compared to control (27.8 ± 1.6% vs. 100.0 ± 4.4% for BMP4 antibody after normalization and 61.5 ± 3.8% vs. 100.0 ± 4.4% for Jagged 1 antibody after normalization; Figure 3F and Videos 6, 7 and 8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: BMP4 antibody was able to reduce the vascular permeability to a value even lower than the level detected in presence of iSMCs from young donors.
source: Noteworthy, BMP4 antibody was able to reduce the vascular permeability to a value even lower than the level detected in presence of iSMCs from young donors (indeed we quantified 72.2% decrease in vascular permeability with BMP4 antibody-treated HGPS cells and only 49.3% decrease comparing iSMCs from young vs. HGPS donors).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of permeability data.

claim: There was an increase in the amount of Y658 VE-cadherin (indication of cell-cell junction destabilization) in presence of untreated iSMCs, in agreement with the higher vascular leakiness.
source: However, we did observe an increase in the amount of Y658 VE-cadherin (indication of cell-cell junction destabilization) in presence of untreated iSMCs, in agreement with the higher vascular leakiness (Figure 3G–J).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3G-J.

claim: Primary, healthy VECs upregulated BMP4 and other genes associated with calcification, skeletal system development and extracellular matrix organization when co-cultured with HGPS fibroblasts.
source: Surprisingly, we also found that primary, healthy VECs upregulated BMP4 and other genes associated with calcification, skeletal system development and extracellular matrix organization when co-cultured with HGPS fibroblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, N = 1 biological replicate).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: BMP2 and BMP4 share a 62% sequence similarity and are functionally equivalent.
source: However, we were surprised to find that BMP2 was upregulated in old donors while BMP4 was highly expressed by HGPS cells. BMP2 and BMP4 share a 62% sequence similarity and are functionally equivalent.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about BMP protein family.

claim: BMP2/4 dysregulation might underlie a common mechanism leading to vascular degeneration during physiological aging and disease.
source: Hence, BMP2/4 dysregulation might underlie a common mechanism leading to vascular degeneration during physiological aging and disease.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of BMP2 upregulation in old donors and BMP4 upregulation in HGPS.

claim: BMP4 directly affects the stability of the endothelial barrier by increasing the vascular permeability both in vitro and in vivo.
source: In this context, BMP4 is not only linked to vascular calcification. Indeed, it directly affects the stability of the endothelial barrier by increasing the vascular permeability both in vitro and in vivo (Helbing et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Helbing et al., 2017.
